subtopic_detail: deciding when persistent bilateral middle ear effusion with documented hearing loss crosses from watchful waiting to surgical referral
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-year-old boy referred by his general practitioner. His parents say he turns the television up until the neighbours can hear it, answers with a puzzled look when spoken to from another room, and that his speech is harder for strangers to understand than his older sister's was at the same age. His kindergarten teacher has raised the same concern in writing.

He had three colds over the winter but has never had ear pain, discharge, or fever with them. Audiology has now assessed him three times, with the first assessment four months ago and the most recent one yesterday, and the effusion has been present at every visit. He has no craniofacial anomaly and no chromosomal or syndromic diagnosis. His immunisations are up to date and his growth is tracking along the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: Both tympanic membranes dull and retracted with visible fluid level, no perforation or discharge, normal facial movement
data_table.Audiology: Type B (flat) tympanogram bilaterally at all three visits over four months; pure tone average 32 dB in the better hearing ear
data_table.Development: Speech intelligibility to an unfamiliar listener below the expected level for age; gross motor and social milestones age appropriate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Refer to ear nose and throat for bilateral ventilation tube insertion
options.rationale: Bilateral effusion documented over at least three months with a hearing level worse than 25 to 30 dB in the better ear, together with a speech and educational impact, is the accepted trigger for surgical referral rather than further observation. He meets all three limbs at four months of documented persistence, 32 dB, and independent teacher concern. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media)
source_refs: NICE NG233: Otitis Media with Effusion in Under 12s

options.text: Prescribe intranasal mometasone 50 mcg once daily for three months
options.rationale: Intranasal corticosteroid produces no clinically meaningful improvement in effusion clearance or hearing in randomised trials and delays definitive management by another three months in a child who has already waited four. It is a reasonable adjunct only where coexisting allergic rhinitis is being treated in its own right. (Source: NICE NG233: Otitis Media with Effusion in Under 12s)
source_refs: NICE NG233: Otitis Media with Effusion in Under 12s

options.text: Arrange repeat audiometry and tympanometry after a further three months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for the first three months because most effusions resolve spontaneously, but that window has already closed and a further wait risks entrenching the speech delay. The distinguishing point against the correct option is that observation is time limited, not open ended. (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media)

options.text: Refer to ear nose and throat for adenoidectomy without ventilation tubes
options.rationale: Adenoidectomy alone gives a smaller and slower hearing benefit than ventilation tubes and is added to tubes rather than substituted for them, and then usually at revision surgery or where nasal obstruction dominates. He has no reported snoring or mouth breathing to justify it as the primary procedure. (Source: NICE NG233: Otitis Media with Effusion in Under 12s)
source_refs: NICE NG233: Otitis Media with Effusion in Under 12s

options.text: Prescribe amoxicillin 15 mg/kg orally three times daily for ten days
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not alter the natural history of a non-infected middle ear effusion and this child has had no pain, fever or discharge at any point, so there is no acute infection to treat. This would be the right answer if he presented with an acutely bulging red drum and fever, which is the near pair being tested here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Middle ear effusion after an upper respiratory illness is extremely common in preschool children and the large majority clear without any intervention within three months, which is why the first pass of management is structured waiting with documentation rather than treatment. The decision to operate rests on a triad of persistence beyond three months, a measured bilateral hearing level in the impaired range, and a functional consequence for speech, language or schooling. Children with Down syndrome, cleft palate or existing developmental delay are moved to referral earlier because they tolerate a conductive loss less well. The reason documentation matters is that a single abnormal tympanogram taken during a cold cannot distinguish a transient effusion from a persistent one. Missing a persistent bilateral loss in the preschool years costs language acquisition at exactly the point it is most rapid.
key_points: Type B tympanogram means a flat trace with no compliance peak, indicating fluid behind an intact drum rather than infection.
Three separate documented assessments across at least three months are what convert an effusion from transient to persistent.
A pure tone average worse than 25 to 30 dB in the better hearing ear is the hearing limb of the referral trigger.
Antibiotics, antihistamines, decongestants and intranasal steroids all fail to change the course of a non-infected effusion.
Syndromic children and those with pre-existing developmental delay are referred without waiting the full three months.
explanation.pearls: Autoinflation using a purpose made nasal balloon is the one non-surgical measure with trial support in this setting, giving a modest improvement when performed three times daily for up to three months, and it is worth offering to a co-operative child who is waiting for a surgical list.

sources.label: NICE NG233: Otitis Media with Effusion in Under 12s

subtopic_detail: choosing the confirmatory test after a markedly raised creatine kinase in a boy with late walking and calf hypertrophy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a developmental clinic reviewing a 4-year-old boy whose parents report he did not walk until 19 months and still cannot keep up with other children at kindergarten. His mother says he pushes on his own thighs with his hands to stand up from the floor and that his calves look unusually solid for a boy who runs so little.

His general practitioner ordered bloods when the transaminases came back raised on a screen for recurrent tummy pains. Alanine aminotransferase is 186 U/L (less than 40) and aspartate aminotransferase is 214 U/L (less than 40), but the gamma glutamyl transferase and bilirubin are within normal limits and he has no jaundice or hepatomegaly. A creatine kinase sent on the repeat sample is 14 200 U/L (60 to 305). His speech is mildly delayed and there is no family history of neuromuscular disease.

data_table.Examination: Bulky firm calves bilaterally, proximal lower limb weakness with a positive Gowers manoeuvre, reflexes present at the knees, no fasciculation
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 14 200 U/L (60 to 305), alanine aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 40), gamma glutamyl transferase and bilirubin within normal limits
data_table.Growth: Weight and height both tracking on the 25th centile

lead_in: Which investigation would you arrange to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Nerve conduction studies with concentric needle electromyography of the legs
options.rationale: Electrophysiology separates a neuropathic from a myopathic process but this distinction is already settled by the creatine kinase in the thousands together with the clinical pattern. It is a painful test in a preschool child and would not name the responsible gene. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy)

options.text: Genetic testing for deletions, duplications and sequence variants in the DMD gene
options.rationale: A creatine kinase in the thousands with proximal weakness and calf hypertrophy in a boy of this age points to a dystrophinopathy, and targeted DMD analysis identifies a deletion or duplication in around 70 per cent with sequencing finding most of the remainder. Naming the variant also determines eligibility for exon skipping therapy and allows carrier testing for the mother and her sisters. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy)
source_refs: Genetics in Medicine: DMD Diagnostic Care Considerations

options.text: Liver ultrasound with a fasting metabolic screen for a glycogen storage disorder
options.rationale: The raised transaminases came from muscle rather than liver, which the normal gamma glutamyl transferase and bilirubin already establish, so a hepatic workup chases a result that is not hepatic in origin. This is the common trap that delays the diagnosis by months when a child is referred to gastroenterology first. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy)

options.text: Open muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis for dystrophin immunostaining
options.rationale: Biopsy is now reserved for the minority in whom genetic testing is uninformative, because it requires an anaesthetic and a surgical wound to reach an answer that genomic testing usually reaches first. The near pair distinction is that dystrophin immunostaining tells you how much protein is present but not which variant to report for family testing. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of both thighs to map the pattern of muscle involvement
options.rationale: Muscle imaging can show selective fatty replacement and is useful for directing a biopsy in an undiagnosed myopathy, but it never delivers a molecular diagnosis and would simply add a sedated scan. It earns its place in the limb girdle dystrophies where the genetic answer is far less predictable. (Source: RCH CPG: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy)

explanation.summary: Boys with a dystrophinopathy are frequently picked up first through incidentally raised transaminases, because alanine and aspartate aminotransferase are released from skeletal muscle as well as liver and a clinician reasonably reads them as hepatic. The discriminator is a normal gamma glutamyl transferase, which is liver specific and stays normal when the source is muscle. Any boy with late walking, a Gowers manoeuvre or unexplained transaminitis warrants a creatine kinase before any hepatic imaging. Confirmation is molecular in the first instance, with biopsy held back for genetically unresolved cases. Early diagnosis matters because glucocorticoids, cardiac surveillance and spinal monitoring all start on a schedule counted from diagnosis.
key_points: A normal gamma glutamyl transferase alongside raised aminotransferases points the source to muscle rather than liver.
Creatine kinase in Duchenne muscular dystrophy is typically ten to one hundred times the upper limit of normal from birth.
Deletion and duplication analysis of the DMD gene finds about 70 per cent of cases, with sequencing capturing most of the rest.
Calf hypertrophy reflects replacement of muscle by fat and fibrous tissue, not genuine muscle bulk.
Identifying the exact variant determines eligibility for exon skipping agents and enables maternal carrier testing.
explanation.pearls: Glucocorticoids change the trajectory rather than merely the symptoms: prednisolone started around age four to five, before the plateau in motor function, prolongs independent walking by roughly two to three years and delays scoliosis surgery.

sources.label: Genetics in Medicine: DMD Diagnostic Care Considerations

subtopic_detail: first line treatment of asymptomatic low blood glucose in an at risk term newborn who is feeding and rooming in with mother
stem:
You are the paediatric resident called to the postnatal ward at 2 am. A term boy born at 39 weeks weighing 4320 g is now 3 hours old. His mother had diet controlled gestational diabetes and the birth was by uncomplicated vaginal delivery with Apgar scores of 9 and 9.

The midwife has completed a first breastfeed lasting 20 minutes with a good attachment, and the pre feed blood glucose taken immediately before the second feed is 1.9 mmol/L on a laboratory confirmed sample. The baby is pink and warm, is rooting and cueing for a feed, has a normal cry and normal tone, and has had no jitteriness, apnoea or seizure activity. Mother is keen to keep him with her and is expressing colostrum well. There is no maternal medication other than the routine antenatal supplements.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 138, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and rooting, normal tone and cry, no jitteriness or abnormal movements, well perfused with capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Laboratory confirmed blood glucose 1.9 mmol/L at 3 hours of age, taken before the second feed
data_table.Birth details: 39 weeks gestation, birth weight 4320 g, maternal diet controlled gestational diabetes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management of his blood glucose?

options.text: Offer a further breastfeed alone and repeat the blood glucose before the next feed
options.rationale: Feeding alone is the right response at the higher end of the low range, but at 1.9 mmol/L a feed by itself is unlikely to correct the glucose quickly and leaves the baby exposed for a further three hours. Colostrum volumes on day one are measured in millilitres and deliver very little substrate. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Commence hourly formula top ups by bottle and repeat the glucose in 3 hours
options.rationale: Routine formula supplementation is not the first response to a single low reading and undercuts a breastfeed that is already attaching well, and a 3 hour interval is too long to detect a falling glucose. Supplementation has a place only once gel and breastfeeding have failed and the mother has agreed to it. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give 40 per cent dextrose gel buccally and feed, then recheck the glucose in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Buccal dextrose gel with a feed is the first line treatment for an asymptomatic at risk newborn with a low glucose, and it reduces admission to the nursery and separation from the mother without increasing later harm. The recheck at 30 minutes after the gel confirms the response and drives the decision about a second dose. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)
source_refs: Cochrane: Oral Dextrose Gel for Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Transfer to the nursery for an intravenous 10 per cent glucose infusion at maintenance rate
options.rationale: Intravenous glucose is reserved for a baby who is symptomatic, who cannot feed, or whose glucose stays low after adequate gel and feeding, none of which applies to a well baby who is rooting at 3 hours. Starting it here separates mother and baby and undermines the establishment of breastfeeding for no measurable gain. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give a 2 mL/kg intravenous bolus of 10 per cent glucose and admit for observation
options.rationale: A glucose bolus is the treatment for a symptomatic infant with seizures or obtundation, and giving one to an asymptomatic baby provokes rebound insulin release and a second lower trough. The near pair distinction from the correct option is route: buccal absorption raises the glucose without the insulin surge that a rapid intravenous load produces. (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Infants of mothers with any form of diabetes, infants who are large or small for gestational age, preterm infants and unwell infants are all screened for low blood glucose in the first hours of life because transient hyperinsulinism is common and initially silent. The operational threshold used across Australian services is 2.6 mmol/L, with a lower trigger in the first few hours reflecting the physiological nadir that every newborn passes through. Buccal dextrose gel changed practice because it treats the biochemical problem while keeping mother and baby together, which in turn protects breastfeeding. Escalation to intravenous glucose is driven by symptoms or by failure to respond, not by the number alone. Persistent low readings beyond 48 to 72 hours are a different problem and require a hypoglycaemia screen taken at the time of the low glucose.
key_points: Screen at risk newborns before feeds rather than after, since a post feed value can mask the true trough.
The working threshold in Australian neonatal units is 2.6 mmol/L for an at risk but asymptomatic baby.
Buccal 40 per cent dextrose gel with a feed is first line and can be repeated once before escalating.
Jitteriness, apnoea, hypotonia or seizures move the baby straight to intravenous glucose regardless of the number.
Low glucose persisting past 72 hours should prompt a formal hypoglycaemia screen drawn during the episode.
explanation.pearls: Draw the critical hypoglycaemia screen, including insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones and free fatty acids, while the glucose is still below 2.6 mmol/L: once it is corrected the sample no longer distinguishes hyperinsulinism from a fatty acid oxidation defect.

sources.label: Cochrane: Oral Dextrose Gel for Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

subtopic_detail: applying gestational age and birth weight thresholds to decide which preterm infant enters the retinal screening programme and when
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar planning the week's screening list on a tertiary nursery. Four infants are under your care and the ophthalmology service visits every Thursday.

The infant you are asked about was born at 29 weeks and 2 days gestation weighing 1180 g and is now 25 days old, corrected to 32 weeks and 6 days. He needed continuous positive airway pressure for 11 days and two days of supplemental oxygen at 30 per cent, and is now in air and fully enterally fed. He has had no retinal examination since birth. His cranial ultrasound was normal and he has had no culture proven sepsis. The consultant asks you to confirm the timing of his first eye examination before the list is finalised.

data_table.Examination: Settled in an open cot in air, weight now 1560 g, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Birth details: 29 weeks and 2 days gestation, birth weight 1180 g, currently 32 weeks and 6 days corrected
data_table.Respiratory course: Continuous positive airway pressure for 11 days, supplemental oxygen to a maximum of 30 per cent for 2 days, now in air

lead_in: When should his first retinal examination be performed?

options.text: At 36 weeks corrected age once he is established in an open cot in air
options.rationale: Waiting until 36 weeks corrected risks missing aggressive posterior disease, which can reach a treatable stage between 32 and 35 weeks corrected and progress within days. Being in air is a marker of respiratory recovery and has no bearing on when retinal vascularisation becomes visible. (Source: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.text: At discharge from the nursery or at term corrected age, whichever comes first
options.rationale: A discharge examination is the endpoint of a screening series rather than its start, and by term corrected age treatable disease may already have scarred or detached. Screening exists precisely to find disease during the window in which laser or intravitreal therapy still works. (Source: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.text: Only if he requires further supplemental oxygen or develops culture proven sepsis
options.rationale: Oxygen exposure and sepsis worsen the risk but are not the entry criteria, which are gestation below 31 weeks or birth weight at or below 1250 g, and he meets both independently of his oxygen history. Restricting screening to oxygen exposed infants would miss disease in infants who were never ventilated. (Source: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.text: At 4 weeks after birth or 31 weeks corrected age, whichever comes later
options.rationale: Screening starts at 4 weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks corrected gestational age, whichever falls later, which for a 29 week infant means his first examination is due now at 32 weeks and 6 days corrected. Timing it this way catches disease before it becomes treatable rather than after, because vision threatening changes almost never appear before 31 weeks corrected. (Source: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity

options.text: At 6 weeks after birth regardless of the corrected gestational age reached
options.rationale: A fixed postnatal interval ignores the maturity of the retina, so it screens the most immature infants too late while examining more mature ones before there is anything to find. The near pair error is treating postnatal age as the only clock when the schedule deliberately uses two clocks and takes the later of them. (Source: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity)
source_refs: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity

explanation.summary: Retinopathy of prematurity develops because an incompletely vascularised retina is exposed to a relatively hyperoxic extrauterine environment, which first arrests vessel growth and then drives disordered neovascularisation as the retina grows and becomes ischaemic. Australian entry criteria are a gestational age below 31 weeks or a birth weight at or below 1250 g, with clinician discretion to include larger or more mature infants who had an unstable course. The first examination is timed to 4 weeks postnatal or 31 weeks corrected, whichever is later, and subsequent intervals are set by what the ophthalmologist sees, typically every one to two weeks. Treatment with laser or intravitreal anti vascular endothelial growth factor is indicated for type 1 disease and should occur within 72 hours of the decision. The programme only works if the infant is tracked through transfers between hospitals, which is where most failures occur.
key_points: Entry criteria in Australia are gestation under 31 weeks or birth weight at or below 1250 g.
First examination is at 4 weeks postnatal age or 31 weeks corrected age, whichever falls later.
Examination is by indirect ophthalmoscopy with mydriatics, with sucrose and swaddling for comfort.
Type 1 disease requires treatment within 72 hours, most often laser or intravitreal anti vascular endothelial growth factor.
Screening continues until the retina is fully vascularised or the ophthalmologist documents low risk of progression.
explanation.pearls: Aggressive posterior retinopathy can progress from mild to treatment requiring disease in under a week, so an infant with plus disease is reviewed within days rather than at the routine one to two week interval.

sources.label: RANZCO: Screening for Retinopathy of Prematurity

subtopic_detail: selecting the assessment pathway for a child labelled penicillin allergic after a delayed rash during a course of amoxicillin
stem:
You are the general paediatric registrar in clinic. A 5-year-old girl is referred because her record carries a penicillin allergy label that is complicating her care: she has had two courses of a broader agent this year for chest infections and her family is anxious about every prescription.

The label dates from age 2, when she developed a flat pink rash over her trunk and limbs on day 6 of a 10 day course of amoxicillin for an ear infection. Her mother describes it as blotchy and not itchy, says it faded over four days without treatment, and is clear that there was no swelling of the lips or face, no breathing difficulty, and no blistering or peeling anywhere including inside her mouth. She was otherwise well through the episode and did not need to see a doctor urgently. She has taken cefalexin since without any reaction and has no other drug or food allergies.

data_table.Examination: Skin clear today with no rash, no mucosal lesions, chest clear on auscultation
data_table.Reaction details: Flat non urticarial rash on day 6 of a 10 day amoxicillin course at age 2, resolved over 4 days without treatment, no mucosal or systemic features
data_table.Subsequent exposure: Cefalexin tolerated on two occasions since, no reaction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to her penicillin allergy label?

options.text: Arrange skin prick and intradermal testing to penicillin determinants before any challenge
options.rationale: Skin testing is validated for immediate immunoglobulin E mediated reactions such as urticaria, angioedema or anaphylaxis within an hour of a dose, and it neither predicts nor excludes a delayed rash. The near pair distinction is reaction timing: hers began on day 6, which places it outside the mechanism that skin testing interrogates. (Source: ASCIA: Penicillin Allergy De-labelling)

options.text: Measure serum specific immunoglobulin E to penicilloyl determinants and interpret the titre
options.rationale: Specific immunoglobulin E to penicillin has poor sensitivity even in genuine immediate allergy, so a negative result cannot remove a label and a positive one in this context would be a false alarm. Ordering it here tests a mechanism the history has already argued against. (Source: ASCIA: Penicillin Allergy De-labelling)

options.text: Retain the label permanently and continue to prescribe non penicillin agents when required
options.rationale: An unexamined label is not a neutral act: it drives use of broader agents with more resistance selection, more adverse effects and higher cost, and around nine in ten labelled children are not truly allergic. This is the anti-pattern the referral was made to correct. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Begin a graded oral desensitisation protocol with incremental amoxicillin doses over one day
options.rationale: Desensitisation is for a patient with proven allergy who has no alternative agent, and it induces temporary tolerance that is lost once the drug is stopped rather than removing the label. Using it here would treat a diagnosis that has not been established. (Source: ASCIA: Penicillin Allergy De-labelling)

options.text: Arrange a direct oral amoxicillin challenge under observation without prior skin testing
options.rationale: A benign delayed non urticarial rash appearing after several days of a penicillin, with no mucosal, systemic or blistering features, is a low risk history and is assessed by direct oral challenge rather than by skin testing. Australian de-labelling pathways use this route because skin testing has no predictive value for delayed T cell mediated rashes and adds cost and delay. (Source: ASCIA: Penicillin Allergy De-labelling)

explanation.summary: Around one in ten children carry a penicillin allergy label, yet fewer than one in ten of those labels survives formal assessment, and most originate in a viral exanthem that coincided with an antibiotic course. Risk stratification is by history alone in the first instance: timing from the dose, morphology of the rash, and the presence or absence of mucosal involvement, blistering, organ involvement or cardiovascular compromise. Low risk histories such as a delayed benign maculopapular rash in a well child proceed to direct oral challenge, which is safe to perform in a suitably equipped outpatient setting. Histories suggesting immediate reactions go to specialist skin testing first, and histories of severe cutaneous adverse reactions are never challenged at all. Removing an incorrect label restores access to narrow spectrum first line therapy for the rest of the child's life.
key_points: Timing separates mechanisms: within one hour suggests immunoglobulin E mediated, after several days suggests a T cell mediated rash.
Direct oral challenge without skin testing is the pathway for low risk delayed benign rashes.
Mucosal involvement, blistering, skin pain or organ dysfunction are absolute contraindications to challenge.
Skin testing and specific immunoglobulin E only address immediate reactions and cannot clear a delayed rash.
De-labelling reduces use of broader agents such as macrolides, cephalosporins and glycopeptides.
explanation.pearls: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions, meaning Stevens Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, are a permanent bar to re-challenge, and the clues that separate them from a benign rash are mucosal ulceration, skin pain, facial oedema and fever beyond day 7.

subtopic_detail: sequencing treatment against imaging after an abnormal newborn screening thyroid stimulating hormone result
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar telephoned by the newborn screening laboratory about a 9-day-old girl born at term. The screening card taken on day 3 showed a thyroid stimulating hormone above the action threshold and a venous confirmatory sample drawn yesterday shows thyroid stimulating hormone 84 mIU/L (1.7 to 9.1) with a free thyroxine of 7.2 pmol/L (10 to 26).

She is feeding every three hours, has regained her birth weight, and opened her bowels this morning. On examination she has a small anterior fontanelle, no goitre, no umbilical hernia and normal tone. The parents are in the department now and are asking what happens next. Your hospital can perform a thyroid ultrasound today but the nuclear medicine department cannot offer a radionuclide uptake scan until next Tuesday, which is six days away.

data_table.Examination: No goitre, no umbilical hernia, normal tone and activity, anterior fontanelle small, weight back to birth weight at day 9
data_table.Investigations: Venous thyroid stimulating hormone 84 mIU/L (1.7 to 9.1), free thyroxine 7.2 pmol/L (10 to 26)
data_table.Logistics: Thyroid ultrasound available today, radionuclide uptake scan not available for 6 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral thyroxine today and arrange imaging without letting it delay treatment
options.rationale: Treatment is started as soon as the venous result confirms the diagnosis, ideally within the first two weeks of life, because the developing brain depends on thyroxine and every week of delay costs cognitive outcome. Imaging defines the underlying aetiology and guides later counselling but never justifies withholding the hormone. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism)

options.text: Wait for the radionuclide uptake scan next Tuesday and start thyroxine once the aetiology is known
options.rationale: Deferring treatment for six days to obtain an aetiological scan inverts the priority, since knowing whether the gland is absent, ectopic or dyshormonogenetic changes nothing about the initial dose. The near pair distinction is that a scan can still be done after treatment starts if performed within the first few days, and if the window is missed the question can be revisited by a trial off treatment at age three. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism)

options.text: Repeat the thyroid function tests in two weeks and treat only if the results remain abnormal
options.rationale: A confirmatory venous sample with this degree of abnormality is diagnostic and does not need a second confirmation, and a further two weeks of untreated hypothyroidism falls outside the window in which outcomes are preserved. Repeat testing is appropriate only for borderline elevations near the action threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism)

options.text: Measure maternal thyroid antibodies and withhold treatment pending the antibody result
options.rationale: Maternal blocking antibodies cause a transient form that is worth identifying, but the antibody result takes days and the infant needs thyroxine whether the cause is transient or permanent. Antibody testing informs the later decision about a trial off treatment, not the decision today. (Source: ESPE: Congenital Hypothyroidism Consensus)

options.text: Start oral iodine supplementation and review the thyroid function tests in one week
options.rationale: Iodine deficiency is a population level cause of hypothyroidism in iodine deplete regions and is not the mechanism in an Australian newborn with a low free thyroxine and a high thyroid stimulating hormone. Supplementing iodine would leave her hypothyroid for another week. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism)

explanation.summary: Congenital hypothyroidism affects roughly one in 2000 to 3000 births and is the most successful condition on the newborn screening panel precisely because treatment is cheap, effective, and time critical. Affected newborns look entirely normal at birth, since maternal thyroxine crosses the placenta and masks the deficit, which is why screening rather than clinical detection drives diagnosis. The screening card measures thyroid stimulating hormone, so the primary gland disorders that make up the great majority are detected while rare central hypothyroidism is missed. Treatment is thyroxine started within the first two weeks, with the dose titrated to keep free thyroxine in the upper half of the reference range and thyroid stimulating hormone suppressed. Aetiological imaging, whether ultrasound or radionuclide scan, is useful but always subordinate to starting treatment.
key_points: Newborn screening measures thyroid stimulating hormone, so central hypothyroidism is not detected by the card.
Affected infants appear clinically normal at birth because maternal thyroxine crosses the placenta.
Thyroxine should begin within the first two weeks of life, at a starting dose of 10 to 15 micrograms per kilogram daily.
Titrate to a free thyroxine in the upper half of the reference range rather than to the thyroid stimulating hormone alone.
A trial off treatment at around age three distinguishes permanent from transient disease when imaging was not diagnostic.
explanation.pearls: Thyroxine tablets are crushed and given in a small volume of water rather than mixed into a bottle of formula, because soy protein, calcium and iron all bind thyroxine in the gut and can halve the absorbed dose.

subtopic_detail: managing falling urine output and a falling haemoglobin in the week after bloody diarrhoea in a preschool child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department. A 3-year-old girl is brought back by her parents seven days after she began having loose stools with blood in them, which settled four days ago. Her mother says she has been drinking but has only had one wet nappy since yesterday morning and that her face looks puffy in the mornings.

She attends a day care centre where two other children had a similar illness after a farm visit. She looks pale and tired but is alert and answering questions. Her stool culture from the first presentation has grown a Shiga toxin producing organism, reported this morning. Her blood film shows fragmented red cells, her platelet count is 42 x10^9/L (150 to 400), haemoglobin 78 g/L (110 to 140) and creatinine 138 micromol/L (20 to 45). Her direct antiglobulin test is negative and her coagulation profile is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 124, blood pressure 112/74, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale, periorbital puffiness, mild pitting oedema to the ankles, abdomen soft and non tender, no purpura
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L (110 to 140), platelets 42 x10^9/L (150 to 400), creatinine 138 micromol/L (20 to 45), fragmented red cells on film, direct antiglobulin test negative, coagulation profile within normal limits
data_table.Microbiology: Stool culture positive for a Shiga toxin producing organism

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Loperamide with generous oral rehydration to reduce stool losses and restore urine output
options.rationale: Antimotility agents prolong contact between toxin and gut mucosa and raise the risk of progression, and her oliguria reflects renal injury rather than ongoing losses so pushing oral fluid risks overload. Her diarrhoea has in any case already settled, which removes the stated indication. (Source: RCH CPG: Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome)

options.text: Supportive care with careful fluid and electrolyte management and paediatric nephrology involvement
options.rationale: Management is supportive, centring on meticulous fluid balance, correction of electrolyte disturbance, transfusion when indicated and early nephrology input for possible dialysis, because no specific therapy shortens the illness. Most children recover renal function with this approach, and the work of the admission is anticipating hyperkalaemia, hypertension and fluid overload rather than treating the organism. (Source: RCH CPG: Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone to clear the organism and shorten the duration of the illness
options.rationale: Antibiotics given in this setting increase toxin release from dying organisms and are associated with a higher rate of progression to the full syndrome, so they are actively avoided unless another infection demands them. This is the central anti-pattern of the presentation: the positive culture invites treatment that makes the outcome worse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: High dose intravenous methylprednisolone followed by a weaning course of oral prednisolone
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no role because the process is toxin mediated endothelial injury rather than immune mediated inflammation, and immunosuppression adds infection risk during an acute illness. The near pair being tested is the immune mediated thrombotic microangiopathy, where plasma exchange and immunosuppression do have a place. (Source: RCH CPG: Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome)

options.text: Urgent platelet transfusion to correct the thrombocytopenia before any further intervention
options.rationale: Platelets are consumed within microthrombi rather than failing to be produced, so transfused platelets fuel further thrombosis and are withheld unless there is active bleeding or a procedure is planned. She has no purpura and no bleeding, which is the finding that removes the indication. (Source: RCH CPG: Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome)

explanation.summary: The diarrhoea associated thrombotic microangiopathy of childhood follows infection with Shiga toxin producing bacteria acquired from undercooked meat, unpasteurised dairy, contaminated water or direct animal contact, and characteristically declares itself five to ten days after the diarrhoea begins, often as the bowel symptoms are improving. The diagnostic triad is microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with fragmented red cells, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury, and the negative direct antiglobulin test is what separates this mechanical haemolysis from an immune one. Around half of affected children need dialysis during the acute phase, yet the large majority recover renal function. Treatment is entirely supportive, and the two interventions that feel most natural, antibiotics and antimotility agents, both worsen outcomes. Long term follow up is required because a minority develop hypertension, proteinuria or chronic kidney disease years later.
key_points: Onset is typically five to ten days after the onset of bloody diarrhoea, often as stools are settling.
A negative direct antiglobulin test distinguishes this mechanical haemolysis from autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.
Antibiotics and antimotility agents both increase the risk of progression and are avoided.
Platelets are transfused only for active bleeding or before a procedure, since they feed ongoing microthrombosis.
Annual review of blood pressure and urinalysis is needed for years after apparent recovery.
explanation.pearls: Eculizumab is reserved for complement mediated disease rather than the Shiga toxin form, and because it blocks terminal complement the child needs meningococcal vaccination plus antibiotic cover before the first dose.
